blocks.prompt: The Tractor That Was Built to Be Slow
blocks.text: A tractor has one job. It pulls. It pulls a plow that cuts the dirt. It pulls a mower that cuts the grass. It pulls a wagon full of hay. To pull hard, a tractor needs to push down hard. So the back wheels are huge and heavy. They grip the ground like big rubber boots. Look at the deep lines on the tire. They are called lugs. The lugs bite into the soft dirt. Mud falls out of them as the wheel turns. A tractor is slow, and that is on purpose. Slow is how it pulls.

blocks.prompt: Why a Tractor Is Slow on Purpose
blocks.text: A race car and a tractor both have engines. But they are built for opposite jobs. A race car turns its engine power into speed. A tractor turns its engine power into pulling. It cannot do both at once. Inside a tractor there are gears. The gears let the engine spin many times while the wheels turn only once. Every extra spin adds twisting force. That trade is simple. The tractor gives up speed and gets strength. Most tractors work a field at about four miles an hour, slower than a bike. Pulling also needs grip. A wheel can only pull as hard as it can hold on. So a tractor keeps its weight over the back wheels, and those wheels are made huge. Some farmers even fill the tires with water to make them heavier. The deep rubber bars on the tire are called lugs. They bite into the soil, and they throw the mud out as the wheel spins, so they stay clean. A tractor is slow the way an ox is slow. Not because it is weak. Because slow is where the strength lives.

blocks.prompt: Before Tractors, the Horse
blocks.text: For thousands of years, the most powerful thing on a farm was an animal. A farmer with a team of horses could plow about an acre in a long day, and the horses had to be fed whether they worked or not. Roughly a quarter of American farmland was planted just to grow food for the animals doing the work. Steam engines came first. They could pull, but they were enormous, heavy enough to sink in wet ground, and they needed a crew to feed the fire. In 1892, in Iowa, a man named John Froelich mounted a gasoline engine on a running gear and built a machine that could drive forward, drive backward, and pull. It is usually called the first successful gasoline tractor. The machine that actually reached ordinary farms was Henry Ford's Fordson, mass produced starting in 1917. It was small, cheap, and built on an assembly line, and it put pulling power within reach of a normal family farm. Then came a second idea that mattered as much as the engine. A shaft at the back of the tractor, called the power take off, let the engine spin a machine instead of just dragging it. Now the tractor could run a mower, a baler, a pump. The tractor stopped being a metal horse. It became the farm's engine, and everything else plugged into it.

notes: Harry Ferguson built the three point hitch in the 1920s and 1930s

blocks.prompt: The Trick That Pushed Down While It Pulled
blocks.text: Early tractors had a dangerous habit. A farmer would chain a plow to the back of the machine, high up near the axle, and start pulling. If the plow struck a rock and stopped dead, the tractor did not stop. The rear wheels kept turning, the whole machine rotated backward around its own axle, and it flipped over on top of the driver. Fordsons killed people this way. The physics is simple and unforgiving: pull from a point above the axle and the machine wants to rear up like a horse. An Irish engineer named Harry Ferguson spent years on the problem, and in the 1920s and 1930s he worked out something better than a chain. He mounted the plow on three arms, two low and one high, so the tractor and the tool became one rigid body instead of two things dragging each other. The lower arms pulled from below the axle line. Now, when the plow snagged, the force pressed the front of the tractor down instead of lifting it up. Then Ferguson added the clever part. He linked those arms to a hydraulic system that could feel how hard the soil was resisting. When the plow bit deeper and the pull grew heavier, the linkage transferred some of the plow's weight onto the rear wheels. The harder the ground fought back, the harder the tractor pressed down, and the more grip it found. The system fed on its own struggle. That idea is called draft control, and the whole arrangement is the three point hitch. It made a small light tractor do work that used to need a big heavy one, and it made a tool that had killed farmers into a tool that steadied itself. Look at the back of almost any tractor built since. You will find the same three arms. Ferguson's design was so plainly right that the industry simply adopted it, and it is still standard equipment nearly a century later.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: From the Latin trahere, to pull
Field speed is about four to six miles an hour
The Ferguson System: three point hitch plus draft control

blocks.prompt: The Slow Machine That Rebuilt the Countryside
blocks.text: A tractor is a strange kind of vehicle, because it is not really built to travel. A car spends its engine on speed. A tractor spends its engine on force, and in a working field it rarely exceeds five miles an hour. That is not a shortcoming that engineers failed to fix. It is the entire design. The reason sits in the gearbox. Gears trade one thing for another: let the engine spin many times for every single turn of the wheel, and the twisting force at the wheel multiplies. Speed goes down, pulling force goes up. But force at the wheel is worthless if the wheel cannot hold the ground. A tire can only pull as hard as friction lets it, and friction grows with the weight pressing the tire into the soil. This is why a tractor looks the way it does. The rear wheels are enormous, the weight is carried over them, the tread bars are deep enough to bite, and farmers still add iron weights or fill the tires with liquid to make them heavier. Every design choice serves grip. For thirty years, that grip came with a body count. Early tractors hitched their plows high, near the axle. When a plow caught a root and stopped, the spinning rear wheels drove the whole tractor to rotate backward around its own axle and land on the driver. Harry Ferguson, an Irish engineer, solved it in the 1920s and 1930s with three arms instead of a chain. Two low arms pulled from beneath the axle line, so a snagged plow pressed the tractor's nose down rather than lifting it. Better still, he tied the linkage to hydraulics that sensed the soil's resistance and shifted part of the implement's weight onto the rear wheels as the pull increased. The harder the field resisted, the harder the tractor gripped. That is draft control, and Ferguson's three point hitch is still bolted to the back of nearly every tractor made today. What followed was not really an agricultural story. In 1900, close to forty percent of Americans worked on farms, and a quarter of the cropland existed only to feed the horses and mules doing the pulling. A team could plow perhaps an acre in a hard day. Machines that never tired, never ate, and never needed a pasture broke that arithmetic. Today fewer than two percent of Americans farm, and they feed far more people than the forty percent ever did. The tractor did not just change farming. It emptied the countryside and filled the cities, and almost nobody voted on it. The newest tractors steer themselves. Satellite guidance can hold a machine on a line within an inch, pass after pass, straighter than any human hand. The driver is there to watch. But the same engineering logic that made tractors strong has made them huge, and huge machines press down on soil that was never meant to be pressed. Compacted ground drains badly and chokes roots, and the damage can reach deeper than a plow will ever reach. So the problem has quietly turned itself inside out. For a century, the great question was how to get enough weight onto the wheels. Now some of the best minds in farming are asking how to take it back off.
